Redwood Inference for Financial Services
Private Deployments (VPC / On‑prem)
Production-grade LLM inference with deployment flexibility for regulated environments.

---

Summary
Redwood Inference helps financial services teams run and optimize large language model (LLM) inference with predictable performance, strong operational controls, and flexible deployment options. Redwood Private enables you to deploy Redwood’s inference platform in your VPC (and, when required, on-prem) while maintaining consistent APIs, observability, and rollout tooling.

This one‑pager highlights:
• Reference architecture (VPC / private networking)
• Security & compliance controls (audit logging, SSO/SAML, KMS/HSM integrations)
• A short pilot plan (2–4 weeks) to validate performance + controls
• Example SLO targets used by similar regulated evaluations

---

Who this is for (Financial Services)
Typical teams evaluating Redwood Private:
• CISO / Security Engineering: auditability, encryption, identity controls, evidence requests
• Platform / ML Engineering: latency + throughput, predictable capacity, integration into internal platforms
• Risk / Compliance: data boundaries, retention/residency, governance and change control
• Procurement: commercial structure, SLA, support model

Common finserv workloads we see:
• Internal knowledge assistants (policy/procedure, operations runbooks)
• Customer support copilot (with strict PII controls)
• Fraud ops / investigations assistance (triage and summarization)
• Document understanding and extraction (statements, disputes, onboarding)

---

Why Redwood (for regulated inference)
1) Deployment flexibility without changing your app
• Same core API surface and operational model across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.
• Private options for VPC deployments and on‑prem constraints (scope confirmed during discovery).

2) Production economics: latency + throughput + unit cost controls
• High-throughput runtime with batching, caching, and performance tuning options.
• Token-level observability and cost attribution (per route/model) via Redwood Console.

3) Reliability and operational tooling
• Rollouts (canary / phased), model version pinning, and fallback policies.
• Clear levers to trade off latency vs cost while staying within guardrails.

---

Reference architecture (described)
Below is a typical Redwood Private deployment in a customer-controlled VPC.

[DIAGRAM PLACEHOLDER]

Text description (VPC deployment):
1) Client apps (internal services, web apps, batch workers) call your internal inference endpoint.
2) Traffic enters your VPC through a private ingress (e.g., internal load balancer) with TLS.
3) Requests route to Redwood Inference Runtime (GPU node groups) running inside your private subnets.
4) Optional policy/routing layer applies:
   • model selection (pinned version or approved set)
   • rate limits/quotas by app/team
   • fallback model policy (pre-approved variants)
5) Logs/metrics exported to your tooling:
   • audit logs → SIEM (e.g., Splunk/ELK) via customer-controlled export
   • metrics/traces → your observability stack (plus Redwood Console if enabled)
6) Encryption & keys:
   • data at rest encrypted
   • key management integrated with your KMS (cloud) or HSM-backed systems where applicable
7) Networking boundaries:
   • no public inbound required for the serving path in a private VPC setup
   • egress policies controlled by customer (as needed for model/artifact updates)

On‑prem option (when required):
• Redwood can support on‑prem packaging patterns for regulated/air‑gapped requirements; exact topology, update/upgrade process, and operational responsibilities are confirmed case-by-case.

---

Security & compliance controls (high-level)
Note: The items below describe typical capabilities and deployment patterns. Final scope depends on configuration and contracted terms. Detailed evidence (reports, diagrams, sample logs) is available under NDA via the security evidence pack.

Identity & access
• RBAC for platform access (role-based permissions)
• SSO support (SAML-based) and user lifecycle integration patterns (SCIM where applicable)
• Principle-of-least-privilege guidance for operators and service accounts

Encryption & key management
• Encryption in transit (TLS)
• Encryption at rest for persisted data as configured
• Integrations with customer-managed key systems (KMS) and HSM-aligned patterns depending on environment

Audit logging & monitoring
• Audit events designed to support compliance review and incident investigation
• Export patterns for audit logs to customer-controlled destinations (SIEM/log archive)
• Operational metrics for latency/throughput/error rates, plus request tracing hooks

Data handling controls
• Configurable retention controls aligned with deployment mode and customer requirements
• Data residency/region alignment for VPC deployments (region selection + network boundaries)
• Support for separating environments (dev/test/prod) with clear access and logging boundaries

Security program posture (availability under NDA)
• SOC 2 / ISO posture and current certifications are shared via the evidence pack and security review process.

---

Operational controls for finserv change management
• Version pinning: lock to a model version and rollout intentionally.
• Canary + phased rollouts: reduce regression risk and satisfy change control needs.
• A/B testing: evaluate quality differences against approved prompt sets.
• Automated fallback policies (pre-approved models/regions) to maintain availability.

---

Pilot plan (2–4 weeks)
Goal: validate (1) performance economics, (2) security/compliance controls, and (3) integration effort for a production pathway.

Recommended pilot structure
Week 0 (Prep — 3–5 business days)
• Scope use case: choose 1–2 workflows and success criteria
• Confirm deployment topology (VPC vs on‑prem), networking, and identity requirements
• Security intake: align on evidence pack, questionnaire approach, and timelines

Weeks 1–2 (Integration + baseline)
• Integrate SDK/API with one service (or a thin gateway)
• Implement logging/export and identity access pattern
• Baseline latency/throughput for representative prompts + token distributions

Weeks 3–4 (Hardening + evaluation)
• Add routing/fallback + rollout policies
• Run evaluation set for quality and cost
• Produce a joint readout: results + production proposal (SLOs, capacity, support plan)

Pilot deliverables (what you get)
• Reference architecture aligned to your constraints
• Benchmark summary (p50/p95 latency, throughput, cost drivers)
• Security review packet mapping (controls + evidence index)
• Production rollout recommendation (capacity plan + SLO proposal)

---

Sample SLO targets (illustrative)
Final SLOs depend on model choice, sequence lengths, deployment size, region, and integration path. The targets below are examples used for initial planning and are validated during pilot.

Interactive chat / agentic workflows
• Availability: 99.9% monthly (target)
• Latency (time-to-first-token): p50 < 300–600 ms; p95 < 1.2–2.0 s
• Token generation: steady-state tokens/sec targets defined per model + batch policy

Batch summarization / document workflows
• Throughput: defined as jobs/minute or tokens/sec aggregate
• Completion latency: p95 within agreed batch windows (e.g., < 5–15 minutes for N documents)

Operational SLOs
• Error rate: < 0.1–0.5% (excluding client/network errors)
• Incident response: severity-based response times per support tier

---

What we need from you (to move fast)
• Target workload definition: prompt shapes, max tokens, expected concurrency, and success criteria
• Security contact + questionnaire timeline
• Preferred deployment model: VPC region(s), network constraints, and key management requirements
• Example evaluation dataset (or a safe synthetic set) and governance for handling it
